figures.caption: Table 1: Results on VLA Benchmarks. We report action success rates, where * indicates reproduced results. DRIFT-MLP and DRIFT-Tokenizer use MLP and tokenization-based base predictors, respectively. Across Libero and Simpler benchmarks, DRIFT consistently improves upon OpenVLA and achieves state-of-the-art performance with the Qwen3-VL-2B backbone.

Figure 1: (1): DRIFT learns a velocity field that transports a starting distribution centered at an initial coarse prediction toward the target distribution, simplifying optimization by modeling localized residuals. (2, 3): Visualization of predicted action trajectories (on Libero-Long) and temporal event boundaries (on Charades-STA) under different decoding strategies. Compared to MLP or flow matching, DRIFT produces more accurate and stable predictions with lower variance.

Table 2: Results on Temporal Video Grounding. We evaluate the zero-shot generalization capability of DRIFT on the Charades-STA [12] and ActivityNet Captions [21] test splits, and compare against existing baselines. We report Recall@1 at IoU thresholds ∈ 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 together with mean IoU (mIoU). Baseline results are taken from ED-VTG [44], except for ET-Chat, whose results are reproduced using the released checkpoint under the same evaluation protocol. “# Train” denotes the size of the temporal grounding adaptation corpus. DRIFT outperforms ED-VTG, the strongest generalist baseline, on both datasets, with the largest gains observed on R@1@0.3 and mIoU metrics.

Figure 3: Qualitative Results. Left: Integrating a base predictor and a flow-based refiner enables DRIFT to generate more accurate and stable action trajectories, improving action precision and overall task success rates. Right: Through iterative refinement of the coarse prediction, DRIFT produces sharper and more accurate event temporal boundaries.

Figure 2: (1): Overview of DRIFT, which combines a base predictor with a generative refinement module for continuous decoding conditioned on VLM embedding z. (2): Toy experiments on a synthetic 2D dataset projected into a high-dimensional space with a fixed, random, column-orthogonal projection matrix, following [24]. A 3-layer MLP is trained to model the velocity field in the projected space. The projection matrix is unknown to the model, and only used for visualizing the output. (2-Left): DRIFT achieves faster convergence than flow matching. (2-Right): As the underlying distribution becomes increasingly multimodal, DRIFT more accurately recovers the target distribution.

Table 5: Ablation Studies on Libero-Long. (a) DRIFT outperforms MLP, diffusion, and flowbased decoders. (b) Joint training improves the action representations. (c) The best-performing configuration uses DRIFT with x-prediction and a skip connection.
Figure 4: The overview of the DRIFT’s structure.
